title: Frailty Recognition via Artificial Intelligence: Listening as a Targeted Yardstick in Chronic Heart Failure
summary:
People with chronic heart failure frequently experience reduced physical and mental resilience, a condition known as frailty. Identifying frailty is important for medical care but currently requires time-consuming assessments.

The FRAILTY study investigates whether artificial intelligence (AI) can detect signs of frailty from short voice recordings. Additionally, the study explores whether computer-based analysis of walking patterns and facial movements provides further information.

A total of 250 adults with chronic heart failure will participate. In addition to voice and video recordings, participants undergo assessments of physical performance, muscle strength, mobility, cognitive function, and independence in daily activities. Optional blood samples are collected to investigate potential biological associations. A follow-up assessment is conducted after six months.

The long-term goal is to develop simpler, faster, and non-invasive approaches for detecting frailty. Participation does not affect routine medical treatment.

interventions.name: Prospective, single-arm observational cohort including 250 adults with chronic heart failure. Baseline assessments include clinical frailty evaluation (Clinical Frailty Scale), standardized questionnaires and functional tests, voice recordings, video-based gait and movement analysis, and standardize

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Documented chronic heart failure, irrespective of etiology, left ventricular ejection fraction, or existing cardiac device therapy

Ability to provide independent written informed consent

Sufficient German language proficiency to complete standardized voice tasks and clinical assessments
Exclusion criteria:
- Acute clinical instability or ongoing acute heart failure decompensation at the time of assessment
- Inability to provide independent informed consent
- Insufficient German language proficiency for valid completion of voice and cognitive assessments
- History of heart or other organ transplantation with ongoing systemic immunosuppression
- Inability to obtain technically adequate recordings using the standardized voice protocol
